title: Layer normalisation
objectives: Write layer normalisation with its backward pass, and say when it is preferred to batch normalisation.

screens.title: A batch of one, again
screens.prose: Batch norm on a batch of one erases the input. Text models also see sequences of different lengths, so a "batch statistic" mixes positions and examples. Another way: normalise each example over its own features, one row at a time.

state.caption: Batch norm averages down each column; layer norm across each row.

screens.question: Normalised across its own features, what happens to a single example?

options.text: Its features get mean 0 and sd 1, on its own
It is erased, as with batch norm
options.why: Its features differ from one another, so their spread is not 0.

options.text: It still depends on the other examples
options.why: Only its own features enter its mean and variance.

options.text: Nothing changes: one example cannot be normalised
options.why: One example with several features has a mean and a variance of its own.

hints.text: Batch norm averages down a column.
Here we average along the example's own row.
A row of several different numbers has a non-zero spread.

feedback.correct: Each example is normalised by its own features, so it stands alone.
feedback.generic: Not quite. What goes into the mean now?

byKey.erased: That was batch norm's problem; a row has several different features.

explain.text: Averaging along the row uses only that example's features, so a batch of one is fine and no other example matters. That is **layer normalisation**.

screens.title: Normalise one example by hand
screens.prose: Name it: **layer normalisation** (Ba, Kiros and Hinton, 2016) takes each example's feature vector, subtracts its mean, divides by $\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}$ (over its own $D$ features), then applies a learned $\gamma$ and $\beta$ per feature. It keeps no running statistics, so training and inference agree.
screens.question: An example has features $(1, 2, 3, 6)$. What does the 6 become, before $\gamma$ and $\beta$? Give 4 decimal places.

hints.text: The mean is 3.
The variance is $(4 + 1 + 0 + 9)/4 = 3.5$.

feedback.generic: Not quite. Use the example's own mean and variance.

byKey.ddof: You divided by 3; layer norm divides by the number of features, 4.

explain.text: Mean 3, variance 3.5, so 6 becomes $3/1.8708 = 1.6036$. The same input always gives the same output, in training and in use.

screens.title: Which axis
screens.prose: In a sequence model a batch is an array of shape (32, 10, 64): 32 sequences of 10 positions, each a vector of 64 features. Layer norm normalises over the last axis, one vector at a time.
screens.question: How many separate means does one layer-norm call compute on this array?

hints.text: One mean per feature vector.
There is one vector per sequence and position.

feedback.correct: $32 \times 10 = 320$ vectors, each with its own mean over 64 features.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Count the feature vectors.

byKey.feat: 64 is how many numbers each mean averages, not how many means there are.
byKey.all: That counts every number; each mean covers 64 of them.
byKey.batch: Each sequence has 10 positions, each normalised on its own.

explain.text: The last axis is reduced, so the result has shape (32, 10, 1): 320 means. `sequence` L4 puts this op before attention and the MLP in each block (pre-norm residual), and reuses this course's `layernorm`.

screens.title: Layer norm, backward
screens.prose: We derive $\partial L/\partial x_i$ for one feature vector, with $\hat x_i = (x_i - \mu)/s$, $s = \sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}$, and $d_i = \gamma_i\,\partial L/\partial y_i$ the gradient reaching $\hat x_i$.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. Leave out the two that do not belong.

lines.text: $\partial \mu/\partial x_i = 1/D$, since $\mu$ is the mean of $D$ features
$\partial \hat x_j/\partial x_i = \big(\delta_{ij} - \tfrac1D - \tfrac1D\hat x_i\hat x_j\big)/s$, by the quotient rule
$\partial L/\partial x_i = \sum_j d_j\,\partial \hat x_j/\partial x_i$, the chain rule over every $\hat x_j$
$\partial L/\partial x_i = \tfrac1s\big(d_i - \tfrac1D\sum_j d_j - \hat x_i\,\tfrac1D\sum_j d_j\hat x_j\big)$, collecting terms
$\partial L/\partial x_i = d_i/s$, treating $\mu$ and $s$ as constants
lines.why: Every $\hat x_j$ depends on $x_i$ through $\mu$ and $s$, so those paths add terms.

lines.text: $\partial \mu/\partial x_i = 1$, since $x_i$ appears in the mean once

hints.text: Start with how the mean and the scale move with $x_i$.
Then differentiate $\hat x_j$ with the quotient rule.
Finally sum over $j$ and collect.

feedback.correct: Mean and scale first, then the quotient rule, the chain rule, and collecting the sums.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Each line uses the one before.

byKey.x1: That drops the paths through $\mu$ and $s$, which every feature shares.
byKey.x2: The mean weights each feature by $1/D$.

explain.text: Each feature moves the shared mean by $1/D$ and the shared scale by $\hat x_i/D$. Summing those paths subtracts the mean of $d$ and the part of $d$ along $\hat x$.

options.text: Nothing useful: the output is all zeros

options.text: Code that fails on a batch of one at once

hints.text: Which axis does `axis=0` average over?
Axis 0 is the batch.
That is batch norm's statistic.

feedback.correct: Axis 0 is the batch, so this is batch norm in training mode, with all its faults: one example's output depends on the others.

byKey.ln: That is the trap: the same formula over the wrong axis silently becomes batch norm.

explain.text: Layer norm reduces over the last axis, the features of each example. Over axis 0 the same formula is batch norm, and a loss that falls hides the change.

widget.solution:
import numpy as np


def layernorm_forward(x, gamma, beta, eps):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    mu = x.mean(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    var = x.var(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    return gamma * (x - mu) / np.sqrt(var + eps) + beta


def compare_norms(x):
    x = np.asarray(x, dtype=float)
    ln = layernorm_forward(x, 1.0, 0.0, 1e-5)
    bn = (x - x.mean(axis=0)) / np.sqrt(x.var(axis=0) + 1e-5)
    return ln, bn

widget.solution:
import numpy as np
from autograd import Tensor


def layernorm(x, gamma, beta, eps=1e-5):
    d = x.data.shape[-1]
    mu = x.data.mean(axis=-1, keepdims=True)
    inv = 1 / np.sqrt(x.data.var(axis=-1, keepdims=True) + eps)
    xhat = (x.data - mu) * inv
    out = Tensor(gamma.data * xhat + beta.data, (x, gamma, beta), "layernorm")

    def _backward():
        g = out.grad
        lead = tuple(range(g.ndim - 1))
        gamma.grad += (g * xhat).sum(axis=lead) if lead else g * xhat
        beta.grad += g.sum(axis=lead) if lead else g
        dx = g * gamma.data
        x.grad += inv / d * (d * dx - dx.sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True) - xhat * (dx * xhat).sum(axis=-1, keepdims=True))
    out._backward = _backward
    return out

screens.title: Scoring each stock on its own
screens.prose: A model scores each stock every day from its own feature vector, in batches of whatever stocks happen to update together. The desk needs a stock's score not to depend on which others share its batch.
screens.question: Which normalisation meets that, and why?

options.text: Layer norm: each stock is normalised by its own features alone
Batch norm in training mode: it adapts to each day's batch
options.why: That makes a score depend on the batch, exactly what the desk forbids.

options.text: Batch norm in inference mode only, which is as good in training too
options.why: In inference mode it is fixed per row, but training it still mixes the batch, and its running averages drift as the stock universe changes.
Layer norm uses only the row's own features.

hints.text: Which statistic uses only one row?
Layer norm reduces over the features.
So a stock's output ignores the other stocks.

feedback.correct: Layer norm: a stock's score depends on its own feature vector only, in training and in use.
feedback.generic: Not quite. Which norm never looks at other rows?

explain.text: Layer norm's mean and variance come from one stock's features, so batch membership cannot change its score. It needs no running averages either.

ideas: Layer norm normalises each example over its own features (the last axis), then applies $\gamma$ and $\beta$; it has no running averages.
It acts the same in training and inference and never mixes examples, so a batch of one and sequences of any length are fine.
Its backward subtracts the mean of the incoming gradient and its part along $\hat x$; over the wrong axis it silently becomes batch norm.
